title: The Red Spider Nebula: surfing in Sagittarius - not for the faint-hearted!
caption: The Red Spider Nebula, NGC 6537, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 6537, Red Spider Nebula · constellation Sagittarius
credit: ESA & Garrelt Mellema (Leiden University, the Netherlands)

recognition.text: Ranked #31 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble picture shows the Red Spider Nebula, NGC 6537, a two-lobed planetary nebula in the constellation of Sagittarius. According to the caption, it lies some 3000 light-years away. The nebula is sculpted by huge waves.

A planetary nebula forms from the outer layers of a dying star, cast off into space and lit up by the hot core left behind. This warm example holds one of the hottest stars known, and that star's powerful winds drive waves 100 billion kilometers high.

The waves are supersonic shocks. As the lobes expand rapidly, they compress and heat the gas in front of them, much as a fast-moving boat piles up water at its bow. Atoms caught in these shocks give off the radiation that makes the nebula visible, so what we see is essentially a map of where the gas is being struck. The official caption offers no details about the filters or colors used.

understand.summary: This is a Hubble image, but the source gives no instrument or filter information and does not publish the color mapping.
understand.eye: Long telescope exposures gather far more light than the eye, so this faint glowing gas would not look like this by eye.
